passage: Chaitanya's grandmother died two days before Diwali, and the house that had been full of lamps was suddenly full of relatives and quiet. There was no time to grieve: the rituals needed arranging, the priest was double-booked, and it was pouring. His cousin Lalit arrived soaked, holding marigolds. Together they washed the courtyard for the thirteenth-day prayers. Chaitanya kept expecting to hear her calling him to taste the laddoos. During the chanting he cried, and so did Lalit. Afterwards the neighbours came with food, each telling a small story about her: the extra rotis she sent over, the sari she stitched for a bride. Chaitanya listened and felt something loosen. "It still hurts," he said to Lalit that night. "But I feel like she's everywhere in this street." Lalit nodded. "She is."

qa.q: When did Chaitanya's grandmother die?
qa.a: She died two days before Diwali.

qa.q: Why did the neighbours' stories make Chaitanya feel something loosen?
qa.a: Hearing how his grandmother helped others showed that her life still mattered to many people. That shared memory made the grief easier to hold, even though it still hurt.

qa.q: At the prayers, Chaitanya let himself cry instead of holding it in. How did that choice help him through the day?
qa.a: Crying alongside Lalit during the chanting let the grief be shared rather than hidden. Afterwards he was open enough to take comfort from the neighbours.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt arriving soaked with marigolds in the rain?
qa.a: Lalit was grieving too, and helping with the rituals was a way to show love for the grandmother and support Chaitanya. 🤍

grounding: A young man grieving his grandmother finds comfort in the rituals and in the neighbours' stories about her, though it still hurts.

passage: Every Sunday morning since her husband's accident, Nikita had taken the 8 a.m. metro to the community kitchen near Chandni Chowk. She was twenty-five and a widow of eight months. At first she went because her friend Gautam dragged her. Now she went without being asked. She chopped onions next to strangers, stirred huge pots of rajma and handed plates to labourers and old men. Some weeks she still cried on the metro back. One Sunday an elderly man took his plate, looked at her and said, "God bless your hands, beti." Nikita smiled and felt, for a moment, that her grief had somewhere to go. Gautam, drying steel plates, caught her eye. "You okay?" "No," she said honestly. "But this helps. It doesn't make sense of it. It just makes it... carryable."

qa.q: How long had Nikita been a widow?
qa.a: She was a widow of eight months.

qa.q: What did Nikita mean when she called her grief "carryable"?
qa.a: Helping others did not explain or remove the loss, but it gave her pain some purpose and made it possible to live with.

qa.q: At first Gautam dragged Nikita to the kitchen. What changed when she started going on her own?
qa.a: It became her own choice and source of meaning, not just a friend's idea. That is when the work began to comfort her.

qa.q: How might the elderly man's blessing have affected Nikita?
qa.a: It made her feel useful and seen at a time when she felt broken. For a moment, her grief had somewhere to go.

grounding: A young widow finds her grief more bearable through serving food at a community kitchen, though it does not make sense of her loss.

"Naveen, you haven't touched Appa's chair in a month."
"I can't, Suraj. It still smells like him."
"Amma asked if we'd come to the temple with her tomorrow. It's the monthly puja."
"I don't even know if I believe in any of that."
"Me neither, fully. But Amma does. And Appa loved the drive."
Next morning the brothers sat on the cold temple floor with their mother. The bells rang. Naveen found himself saying the words Appa used to mumble.
In the car he said, "I thought it'd make it worse."
"Did it?"
"No. It felt like doing something with him instead of just missing him."
Suraj squeezed his shoulder. "Next month too?"
"Next month too."
That evening Naveen sat in Appa's chair for the first time.

qa.q: What was the occasion at the temple?
qa.a: It was the monthly puja.

qa.q: Why was Naveen unsure about going to the temple?
qa.a: He was not sure he believed in the rituals and feared it would make his grief worse.

qa.q: Naveen chose to go despite his doubts. Why did that choice matter?
qa.a: Joining the ritual with his family let him feel connected to Appa instead of only missing him, and that evening he could finally sit in his father's chair.

qa.q: How might Amma feel seeing both sons with her at the puja?
qa.a: She probably felt comforted and less alone in her grief, sharing something that meant a lot to her and to their father.

grounding: Two brothers grieving their father find comfort in a monthly temple ritual with their mother, even without full faith.

When my Nani died last spring, I stopped going up to the terrace. That was her place. Every morning she scattered rice for the pigeons and left a bowl of water for the street dogs by the gate, and every morning she'd call for me to come and see.
I'm Rajni. For weeks after the funeral I just went to work and came home. Then one morning our neighbour Vishal knocked. He was holding her old steel bowl. "The dogs keep waiting at the gate," he said. "Shall we?"
So we did. Now every morning before the office, I fill the bowl and scatter the rice, and Vishal brings biscuits for the dogs. Sometimes children from the lane come to help.
It doesn't bring her back. Some mornings I still cry on the stairs. But up there, doing what she did, I feel close to her, and less alone.

qa.q: What was Vishal holding when he knocked?
qa.a: He was holding her old steel bowl.

qa.q: Why did Rajni stop going up to the terrace after the funeral?
qa.a: The terrace was Nani's place, so being there without her probably felt too painful and empty.

qa.q: What choice helped Rajni carry the grief a little better?
qa.a: Saying yes to Vishal and taking up Nani's morning ritual gave Rajni a way to feel close to her and to share the loss with others.

qa.q: Why might Vishal have come to the door with the bowl?
qa.a: Vishal may have missed Nani too and noticed the dogs waiting, and offering to do it together was a gentle way to reach Rajni without pushing.

grounding: An adult who lost a grandmother finds comfort in continuing her daily ritual with a neighbour; the grief remains but becomes easier to bear.

Facilitator's notes, Irawati, Thursday bereavement circle, community hall
Sarika, 24, first came to the circle in January, three weeks after her mother died. She sat by the door with her coat on and didn't speak for two sessions. In the third she said only, "Everyone says it gets easier. It doesn't."
Tonight was different. She arrived early and helped me set out the chairs. When a new member, an older man who had lost his wife, sat stiffly by the door just as she once had, Sarika brought him tea and sat beside him. Later she told the group, "My mother fed whoever came to the house. Doing this feels like something she'd do."
She said the loss is still heavy. But she stayed for tea afterwards. I'll ask whether she'd like to help welcome newcomers next month, and keep checking in on how she is.

qa.q: What did Sarika say in the third session?
qa.a: "Everyone says it gets easier. It doesn't."

qa.q: Why does bringing tea to the new member mean something to Sarika?
qa.a: Feeding and welcoming people was what her mother always did, so helping him makes Sarika feel connected to her mother in the middle of the loss.

qa.q: What next step is Irawati planning, and why is it well judged?
qa.a: Irawati will ask if Sarika wants to help welcome newcomers while still checking on her, building on what comforts her without pretending the grief has gone.

qa.q: How might the new member have experienced Sarika sitting beside him?
qa.a: He may have felt less alone and less awkward, seeing someone who understood that stiff first visit and made room for him.

grounding: A facilitator sees a grieving adult find comfort in community and in helping a newcomer, which makes the loss more bearable without removing it.

passage:
Sunday

It's been four months since Papa died. The house is too quiet in the mornings.

Today I lit the lamp in front of his photo, the way Mummy does. At first I only did it because she asked. But now I like it. Ten quiet seconds where I talk to him in my head. It doesn't make it better. But it gives the missing a place to go.

Rekha came in the afternoon and we went to the old-age home where Papa used to volunteer on Sundays. I read the newspaper to Mr Fernandes, like Papa did. He said, "Your father had a funny voice for the headlines." I laughed, then cried a little. Mr Fernandes held my hand.

It still hurts. But on the way home I felt like Papa was a bit closer.

Sudha

qa.q: How long has it been since Sudha's father died?
qa.a: Four months.

qa.q: What does lighting the lamp seem to give Sudha?
qa.a: It gives the missing a place to go, a quiet moment of connection that doesn't remove the grief but makes it more bearable.

qa.q: How did continuing Papa's volunteering help Sudha?
qa.a: Reading to Mr Fernandes as Papa did kept a link to Papa and let Sudha share memories, making the loss feel less lonely.

qa.q: How might Mr Fernandes feel when Sudha reads to him?
qa.a: Mr Fernandes likely feels touched and comforted, sharing memories of Papa and holding Sudha's hand during the tears.

grounding: It shows an adult who finds comfort after losing a father through ritual and helping others, which makes the grief more bearable though it remains.

passage: In the village near Kumbakonam, Leela's mother had taught at the small primary school for thirty years. After she died in the monsoon, Leela came home from Chennai for the rituals and couldn't bring herself to leave. Every morning, the house was too still. Her friend Arohi, a teacher at the same school, asked if she'd help with the reading hour, just for a week. Leela hesitated, then went. The children sat on the mat under the neem tree, as they had with her mother. One small girl said, "Your amma used to do the voices." Leela did the voices. Her throat tightened, but she kept going. In the evening, she lit the lamp at her mother's photo and told her about the children. The grief was still there, heavy. But it had somewhere to sit now.

qa.q: How long had Leela's mother taught at the school?
qa.a: Thirty years.

qa.q: How did Leela feel doing the voices at reading hour?
qa.a: Her throat tightened with grief, but she felt a meaningful connection to her mother in carrying on something she did.

qa.q: Why might the reading hour help Leela bear the loss?
qa.a: Helping the children and continuing her mother's work gave the grief meaning and a place to rest, even though it didn't remove it.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel watching Leela with the children?
qa.a: Arohi likely feels tender and hopeful, glad she found a gentle way to support her friend.

grounding: It shows an adult who, after losing her mother, finds comfort in ritual, community and helping others, making the grief more bearable.

Beatriz's grandmother died in March, in the small flat in Porto where she'd taught Beatriz to make rice pudding. For weeks afterwards Beatriz went to work and came home and sat in the dark.

In May her friend Hana invited her to Sunday mass at her grandmother's old parish. Beatriz wasn't sure she believed any more. She went anyway. The candles, the old ladies who hugged her and said, "Your avó talked about you every week," the same hymns her grandmother hummed while cooking; something eased.

After mass, a volunteer asked if anyone could help at the parish lunch for elderly people living alone. Beatriz stayed. She served soup to a man who kept calling her "menina". He told her about his late wife for twenty minutes.

Walking home, she cried a little. It still hurt. But it hurt in a room full of people, not alone in the dark.

qa.q: Where had Beatriz's grandmother taught her to make rice pudding?
qa.a: In the small flat in Porto.

qa.q: What did Beatriz feel at the parish, and what caused it?
qa.a: Beatriz felt comforted and less alone, hearing the old hymns and being hugged by people who knew her grandmother.

qa.q: Why might serving at the lunch have helped Beatriz?
qa.a: Helping someone else carrying grief gave her a sense of meaning and company, which made her own loss more bearable.

qa.q: What was it like for the man who talked about his late wife?
qa.a: The man may have felt listened to and less lonely, finding comfort in sharing his memories with someone kind.

grounding: An adult grieving a loved one finds comfort in ritual, community and helping others, which makes the loss more bearable.

The community kitchen at the gurdwara starts cutting onions at five in the morning. Pankaj started coming the week after his father's cremation, not because anyone asked, but because home was too quiet.

He wasn't Sikh. Nobody minded. Sabina, who ran the vegetable section, handed him a knife and a sack the first day and didn't ask questions.

For the first few mornings he chopped in silence, eyes stinging from more than onions. Then Sabina mentioned her own mother, gone two years. "Doing something for people helped me," she said. "Not instead of missing her. Alongside."

Pankaj thought of his father, who fed every stray dog on their lane. Serving dal to strangers felt, strangely, like something his father would have done.

On the tenth morning he laughed at something one of the aunties said. It surprised him. The grief was still there when he got home. But he found he could carry it.

qa.q: What time does the community kitchen start cutting onions?
qa.a: The community kitchen starts cutting onions at five in the morning.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel when he laughed on the tenth morning?
qa.a: Pankaj felt surprised, since his grief was still there, but for a moment he felt lighter and connected to others.

qa.q: What did Sabina do that helped Pankaj?
qa.a: Sabina gave him a task without questions and later shared her own loss, showing that helping others can sit alongside missing someone.

qa.q: How might Sabina see Pankaj's early mornings in the kitchen?
qa.a: Sabina probably recognised her own grief in his silence and felt tenderness toward him, which is why she spoke about her mother.

grounding: An adult who has lost his father finds meaning in serving at a community kitchen, which makes the grief bearable.

Dear Harsha,

Thank you for coming to the bhog. I didn't get to talk to you properly, so I'm writing.

You asked how I'm doing. It's been six weeks since Mummy. The first days I couldn't eat or think. Everything felt pointless.

What's helped, a little, is the small things we keep doing. Every evening Dad and I light a diya in her corner and read one shabad she liked. I don't understand all of it, but the sound of it steadies me. On Sundays our neighbours bring food and sit with us and tell stories about her I never knew.

And I've started teaching the maths class she used to take for the kids in our lane. When they get a sum right, I hear her laugh in my head.

None of this brings her back. But it makes the days possible.

Thank you for being there.

Amandeep

qa.q: What do Amandeep and Dad do every evening?
qa.a: Every evening they light a diya in her corner and read one shabad she liked.

qa.q: How does Amandeep feel when reading the shabad each evening?
qa.a: Amandeep feels steadied and a little comforted by the sound of it, even without understanding every word.

qa.q: Why might teaching the maths class help Amandeep grieve?
qa.a: It continues something Mummy cared about and connects Amandeep to her memory, giving the loss some meaning.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Harsha would probably feel moved and grateful to be trusted with it, and glad the small rituals are helping.

grounding: An adult grieving their mother finds some comfort in ritual, community visits and continuing her work with children.

"Eshaan, you asked how I got through the year after Nani died. I'm Rekha, and I'm still getting through it, honestly.
She raised me. When she went, in the winter, the house felt hollow. For weeks I couldn't cook, couldn't pray, couldn't do anything.
What helped first was small. Every evening, I lit the brass lamp in front of her photo, the way she did for forty years. It gave the evening a shape. It felt like she was still part of it.
Then my aunt took me to the old-age home where Nani used to volunteer. The women there knew her. They told me stories about her I'd never heard. I started going on Sundays, reading the newspaper to a lady who can't see well.
It doesn't make the missing stop. Some days I still sit on the floor and cry. But helping someone, and lighting the lamp, make it something I can carry."

qa.q: What did Rekha light every evening?
qa.a: Rekha lit the brass lamp in front of Nani's photo.

qa.q: How did lighting the lamp make Rekha feel?
qa.a: It brought comfort and a sense of connection, as if Nani was still part of the evening, after weeks of feeling hollow.

qa.q: What helped Rekha most, and why?
qa.a: A small ritual, the lamp, and helping others at the old-age home gave the grief a shape and a purpose, making it bearable even though the missing remains.

qa.q: How might the lady who can't see well feel about Rekha's Sunday visits?
qa.a: She would probably feel grateful and cared for, looking forward to hearing the newspaper each week.

I've known Nazia since school, and I was with her the week her father died in March.
For the first month she hardly spoke. She went to work, came home, sat by the window. I didn't know what to say, so I mostly brought food.
Then I noticed small things changing. On Fridays she started going to the mosque with her mother again, something she'd stopped in college. During Ramzan she helped at the community iftar her father used to organise, handing out dates and water at the gate. She told me once, "People keep telling me stories about Abbu. It's like he's still here, in them."
I can't know what grief is like from inside. It hasn't gone. Some evenings I still find her quiet by the window.
But she stands a little straighter at that gate. And last week, for the first time, she laughed telling me one of his jokes.

qa.q: Where did Nazia help during Ramzan?
qa.a: She helped at the community iftar her father used to organise, handing out dates and water at the gate.

qa.q: How do the stories about Abbu seem to make Nazia feel?
qa.a: They seem to comfort her and make her feel connected, as if her father is still present in them.

qa.q: Why might faith and community have helped Nazia?
qa.a: Prayer with her mother and serving at the iftar gave her grief a place and a purpose, which does not remove it but makes it easier to bear.

qa.q: How does the narrator feel watching Nazia over these months?
qa.a: The narrator feels unsure what to say at first and is caring and quietly relieved to see her stand straighter and laugh again.

grounding: It shows, through a friend's account, an adult who lost her father finding comfort in faith, community and helping others, which makes the grief bearable.

Come, sit with an old man for a minute, and I'll tell you about Elizabeth. I'm Tanvir; I ran the bakery on Clarke Street for thirty years, and she lived above it.
She was twenty-five when her mother died. For weeks she barely came down. The lights were on at odd hours.
Then one Sunday she came into the shop and asked if I still gave the leftover bread to the shelter on Mill Road. I said yes. She asked if she could carry it.
She carried it every Sunday after that, and she started staying to help serve. She went back to her mother's church too, sat in the same pew. She told me once, "It still hurts every day. But on Sundays it has somewhere to go."
The grief didn't leave her. But she could live beside it.

qa.q: Where did Tanvir give the leftover bread?
qa.a: He gave it to the shelter on Mill Road.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth mean when she said "on Sundays it has somewhere to go"?
qa.a: She still felt grief every day, but helping at the shelter and sitting in the church gave that grief a place and made it bearable.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Elizabeth's story?
qa.a: The turning point was her asking to carry the bread to the shelter, which led her into helping others and back to her mother's church.

qa.q: How might Tanvir have felt seeing Elizabeth come down that Sunday?
qa.a: Tanvir was likely relieved and touched, after weeks of seeing her lights on at odd hours and her barely coming down.

grounding: A young woman who lost her mother finds comfort in helping at a shelter and returning to church, which makes grief bearable.
